memory_leads.lead: The bridge navigation information chain has distinct owners and responsibilities: master/bridge team decides and monitors the voyage, hydrographic/chart authorities originate navigational information, equipment systems present sensor/chart data, and shore operations may advise but do not collapse onboard navigational responsibility.
Nautical charts and publications are controlled information products whose geographic coverage and currency matter independently from the hardware used to display them.
Chart/publication correction state is a durable readiness category: a chart can exist yet be operationally stale if later hazards, aids, depths or route information have not been incorporated.

A passage or voyage plan is a planned-state artifact linking route legs, hazards, margins, reporting points and contingencies; execution should be compared with the plan rather than treating the realized track as if it were always intended.

Positioning is an information-integrity problem rather than one coordinate feed. Satellite position, heading, speed, radar ranges/bearings, visual or other independent cues can cross-check one another, and degraded or misleading position information should remain an explicit state.

Radar and ARPA-type relative-motion information support collision assessment and navigation in reduced visibility, but interpretation, target acquisition and sensor limitations remain separate from the underlying physical traffic situation.

AIS is a cooperative identity/position/intent information layer, not a complete collision-avoidance truth source; missing, stale or incorrect transmitted data should not be silently treated as equivalent to direct sensing.

Electronic-chart display and integrated navigation systems combine chart, route, position and alarm states; safe use depends on configuration, data currency, sensor inputs and operator interpretation rather than merely whether the system is installed.

Bridge-system integration can create common-mode information risk: several displays may agree because they share one erroneous sensor or data source, so agreement between screens is not independent corroboration.

Heading, speed, depth and other bridge sensor inputs are distinct state variables with different failure/degradation modes; navigation decisions can be impaired even when the primary position display remains available.

Maritime distress, safety and routine communications form a separate information path from navigation sensors. Communications availability affects receipt of warnings, coordination and emergency escalation even when onboard positioning remains intact.

Alarm and watchkeeping workload is part of bridge-system performance: more automation and alerts can improve detection while also creating prioritization, acknowledgement or mode-awareness burdens if many systems demand attention simultaneously.

Degraded-mode fallback is a structural capability: loss or distrust of a digital chart, positioning feed, radar/AIS layer or communication path can require slower speed, larger margins, alternative fixing methods or delay rather than immediate loss of all navigation capability.

The atlas information-known-time theme should include navigation-information vintage: the chart/correction, warning, route plan and sensor state available to the bridge at that moment can differ from what later investigators know.

P024 weather-routing advice only becomes executable through the bridge information stack; forecast quality and navigational information integrity are separate links and should not be collapsed into one route-decision state.

P025 chokepoint arrival and eligibility depend on trustworthy position, ETA, charted restrictions and communications, so managed-transit readiness is partly downstream of the navigation-information chain.

Technology adoption should be represented as changed information workflow and failure modes, not only as installation dates: electronic navigation can improve integration while changing dependence on data currency, software configuration and shared sensors.

Generic VTS/harbor communication and traffic coordination was already captured in P022; P026 retains onboard navigation-information and ship-side communication states rather than another shore-control catalog.
The atlas already names technology/operations as a broad axis; P026 adds only the specific navigation-information chain and its degraded-mode semantics.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Blind memory supports system roles but cannot establish product-specific capability, integration quality or historical fleet penetration.
Standards, carriage requirements, exemptions and implementation dates require claim-scoped regulatory Evidence.
Exact failure chains and accident attribution require contemporaneous casualty investigation Evidence.
Current operational disruptions are outside blind historical-memory scope and require source-first collection.

stop_reason: The navigation-information chain is populated from chart/publication currency and voyage planning through positioning, radar/AIS, electronic integration, communications, alarm/workload and degraded-mode fallback. Further recall becomes equipment-, standard-, version-, rule-, casualty- or provider-specific.
truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no equipment capability, regulatory requirement, chart/version state, navigation failure, casualty cause, GNSS interference event or current service condition is verified.
